items.article: On a Fourth Wing hangover? Here are the best romantasy books to read next, from spicy stories to beloved classics The Standard's journalism is supported by our readers. When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. I would like to be emailed about offers, event and updates from Evening Standard. Read our privacy notice . There comes a time in every avid reader’s life when they must put away serious things and take up more (im)mature ones. Rebecca Yarros’ Fourth Wing was the first novel to shift my perspective on the BookTok-dubbed genre of ‘romantasy’. While I’m not hailing it as a piece of prized literature, I can safely declare it to be an enthralling book with well-developed characters and the perfect balance of romance and fantasy. Chances are you agree, or else you wouldn’t have landed on this article. Yarros’ latest instalment, Threshing Day , was released on 29 September – and if you’ve already torn through its 13 stories, you’re in the right place. Read more: New Fourth Wing book, Threshing Day, has landed with 50% off There’s something inherently healing about loosening one’s grasp on high literature and delving into the murky depths of high fantasy and romance instead. This isn’t to say that some novels which fall within the genre are not, or cannot be, considered high-brow classics – far from it.

items.article: WARNING, DISTRESSING CONTENT After Death Row inmate Christa Pike survived two lethal injections on Wednesday evening (September 30), a doctor has claimed it was doomed from the beginning A top doctor has outlined exactly why Death Row inmate Christa Pike didn’t die during the horrific botched execution attempt and warned she may be too ill to be killed. The convicted murderer was set to be executed by lethal injection in the state of Tennessee on Wednesday (September 30). Pike – who had a last ditch request for clemency refused by Governor Bill Lee – was strapped to the gurney as a team of officials attempted to find a vein for the lethal drug. But after two failed doses of the drug, Pike was reportedly left “thrashing” on the gurney and was later rushed to hospital with potentially life-altering brain damage. Dr. Joel Zivot, a vocal opponent of capital punishment and a member of Pike’s defence team, explained how he believed the execution attempt was doomed from the start. “Lethal injection is not a medical act – and it's a difficult thing to administer,” he said. Dr Zivot revealed that lethal injection involves inserting an intravenous catheter (IV), a delicate procedure performed by trained professionals.

items.article: The Michelin Guide is likely to come to India by the year-end, but will its strict criteria have space for the many types of Indian foods? This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you. Subscribe to enjoy similar stories. Ranjit Mankeshwar is a passionate diner. The Mumbai-based physician is planning a food-focused holiday in Hong Kong. He will browse through the Michelin Guide, pick a restaurant, make a reservation and then book his flight tickets. “For me, the guide is like an entry point (to a city),” says the 59-year-old. On a trip to Bangkok, he planned his itinerary around the Michelin-starred Nusara, Sühring and Potong. Hindustan Times recently reported that a senior tourism ministry official had said the government was in the final stages of signing a deal to bring the Michelin Guide, a globally recognised restaurant rating system, to India. Receiving a Michelin Star or two is considered the high point of a restaurant’s life cycle because the rating criteria is strict and the inspections anonymous. A restaurant could get one star for high-quality cooking worth a stop; two stars for excellent cooking worth a detour; and three stars for exceptional cuisine worth a special journey. Additionally, there’s the Bib Gourmand, a title reserved for budget-friendly places, and an extended list for those with good cooking irrespective of the price. items.text: Want longer hair? Here’s how often you should trim your hair for healthy growth
items.article: If long and healthy hair is on your beauty wish list, it may be time to re-examine your haircut schedule. While the popular saying dictates that routine trims are the key to faster hair growth, there are some important modifications to that information. A haircut cannot make your hair grow, however, a strategic scheduling of visits to the salon can help reduce split ends, breakage, and other problems. But how often should you get your hair cut? Below are some helpful pointers on developing your optimal haircut schedule. There is no scientifically accurate interval for a haircut that would apply to everyone. It depends on your hair type, length, styling, and chemical damage, and how quickly it becomes split. As a rule of thumb: Every 8–12 weeks: A good interval to keep your ends healthy while growing your hair out. Every 10-12 weeks: It is good for people with generally healthy hair that want to maintain their length. Every 6-8 weeks: This is for people who often use styling irons, bleach, colour, or chemicals and have split ends. When needed: It is better to cut unhealthy, split, and brittle hair than to wait for the right time to grow long hair. The only difference is that it helps retain your length instead of growing your hair faster. This is one of the most enduring myths about beauty. Hair grows from the follicle located underneath the scalp. Therefore, cutting the hair will not affect the growth rate of the hair strands, since they still originate from the same point.

items.text: My Son Wanted to Be a Content Creator: The Cost of Chasing Online Fame
items.article: At first, Alex's interest in social media seemed harmless. But it spiraled into obsession and then, on his 20th birthday, he died by suicide. My son, Alexander, became fascinated with YouTube when he was about 10 years old. Like millions of children, he began by watching entertaining videos—sports highlights, challenges and creators whose lives appeared exciting and free. But YouTube was not simply a collection of videos that Alex chose to watch. Its algorithm studied him. It learned what held his attention and kept offering him more. At first, it seemed harmless. Then homework began taking longer, bedtime became later and stopping became difficult. There was always another video. Alex would say that he needed only one more minute, but one video led to another and then another. We had rules in our home, including leaving phones on the counter at night. But ordinary household rules were not designed to compete with platforms engineered to keep children engaged. The phone was only the object. The real power was inside it: the endless feed, the recommendations, the notifications and the promise that something even more exciting was about to appear. As Alex grew older, YouTube was joined by TikTok, Snapchat and other platforms. He was no longer satisfied with watching other people. He wanted to become a content creator himself. items.key: ai:i asked my husband to marry me after just four weeks. i know i was right to take that leap of faith... but this is why i wouldn't be happy if my daughter did the same: eilidh dorgan
items.text: I asked my husband to marry me after just four weeks. I know I was right to take that leap of faith... but this is why I wouldn't be happy if my daughter did the same: EILIDH DORGAN
items.article: Usually when people get engaged it's a cause for celebration. But when I announced my engagement, the reaction from my friends and family was largely 'What?!' Not to mention, 'Who?' Usually when people get engaged it’s a cause for celebration. Family members crack open champagne, and friends video call to celebrate. But when I announced my engagement, the reaction from my friends and family was largely ‘What?!’ Not to mention, ‘Who?’ Yes, who. Because my loved ones had not yet met the man I’d asked to marry me. To be honest, I barely knew him myself. I met Sam in November 2019 and four weeks later, I proposed. It might be surprising he said yes, given we were still relative strangers. Even more surprising is that, seven years on, we’re still together. We celebrated our sixth wedding anniversary last month. I was 31 when we met, and Sam 43. At the time, I was in a weird place. After living in New York with my then-boyfriend of five years, I’d left in a hurry after being fired from a job I loathed and breaking up with said boyfriend after growing apart. Fleeing to London , I’d ended up in a cupboard-sized room in a house share in Camberwell with two girls I barely knew.
